=== PAGE 583 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 145
(a) Strengthen institutional and regulatory frameworks for low-emission climate-resilient
development pathways by mainstreaming climate change into integrated land-use
planning.
(b) Increase the climate resilience of vulnerable rural communities through forest and
landscape restoration and reducing demand for fuelwood.
4. The proposed interventions will target districts along the Congo Nile Divide (CND)
region. Rwanda’s CND, an area of 444,600 hectares (ha), is a high-elevation landscape of
remnant natural forest reserves embedded in a mosaic of intensively managed smallholder
farms and commercial plantations. The CND separates the drainage basins of the Congo and Nile
Rivers. It is part of the Albertine Rift, which is one of the most biologically rich regions in Africa
and “one of the most important regions for conservation” on the continent, containing more
than half of Africa’s birds and 40 per cent of its mammals.
5. Though covering barely 5 per cent of the country, this archipelago of protected forests is
of critical importance for:
(a) Its globally recognized high biodiversity values;
(b) Its role in Rwanda’s acclaimed ecotourism offerings, serving as the primary source of
Rwanda’s foreign revenue and as a major economic development driver;
(c) The ecosystem services provided for surrounding subsistence farmlands as well as
commercial tea and coffee plantations offering employment opportunities for women
while providing the second and third highest sources of foreign revenue;
(d) The regulation of water capture and release to growing urban centres on the CND
periphery, the nation’s extensive river network, and downstream hydroelectric
operations; and
(e) The sequestration and storage of nearly 60 per cent of Rwanda’s national carbon stocks.
6. These values and services are already compromised by a combination of anthropogenic
and climatic factors; they will be much more severely threatened by the potential negative
feedback loops associated with projected climate change impacts. The project will promote an
ecosystem-based approach to forest protection and restoration and will increase the extent and
resilience of forest ecosystems and species, including by functionally linking currently isolated
forest fragments. Through these approaches, the project will protect, restore and rehabilitate
forest ecosystems, thus enhancing biodiversity and reducing key threats while increasing the
provision of critical ecosystem services to strengthen the adaptation of vulnerable communities.
7. Project interventions will directly benefit 1,254,242 people (654,404 women). The
project will also indirectly benefit 9,260,745 people and create approximately 24,212 job
opportunities in forest-dependent communities. The total mitigation impact is estimated to be
1,204,448 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (t CO eq) by 2043.
2
8. The total project financing is USD 50,000,000 with a request for GCF grants of USD
39,056,422. The Rwanda Forestry Authority (RFA), Rwanda Water Board (RWB), Rwanda
Development Board (RDB) and the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda (MOE Rwanda) will
provide co-financing of USD 10,831,308 in grants. MOE Rwanda will also provide an in-kind
contribution of USD 112,271. The project is submitted under environmental and social
safeguards (ESS) category B.

=== PAGE 584 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 146
2.2 Component-by-component analysis
Component 1: Mainstreaming climate adaptation into integrated land-use planning (total cost:
USD 2.9 million; GCF cost: USD 2.9 million)
9. This component aims to integrate climate change adaptation considerations into land-
use planning at the national and subnational levels. The goal is to achieve climate resilience
through collaboration among government agencies, civil society, the private sector and diverse
partners. The component has two main outputs: The first is to develop a climate-resilient land-
use plan for the CND by integrating climate adaptation information into existing land-use
planning efforts. The second aims to strengthen institutional capacities in Rwanda to integrate
biodiversity and climate risks into land-use planning.
Component 2: Forest and landscape management and restoration (total cost: USD 18.9 million;
GCF cost: USD 16.3 million)
10. In this component, targeted interventions will integrate climate change awareness and
adaptation into national forest park planning, policies and management, as well as restore
degraded areas within those parks. These efforts will help sustain the forests’ rich biodiversity,
the lucrative tourism revenues that flow into local and national economies, and the ecosystem
services needed for the climate resilience of vulnerable communities. This suite of activities will
also identify priority areas outside of parks – in remnant natural stands, around wetlands and
along streams – for protection and restoration.
Component 3: Enhancing climate adaptation through resilient livelihoods (total cost: USD 22.6
million; GCF cost: USD 15.3 million)
11. The activities under this component aim to combine environmental conservation with
socioeconomic development, creating a multifaceted approach that resonates with the global
commitment to sustainable growth. They include initiatives such as enhancing and restoring
forest plantations, providing sustainable fuel sources, delivering carbon sequestration benefits
totalling 522,606 t CO eq over 20 years, and developing comprehensive land-use planning. The
2
other activities focus on rural livelihoods, financial services and sustainable farming methods.
12. The component will support reafforestation on steep slopes on both public and
smallholder private lands. It will develop farm-based agroforestry for climate-resilient species
that produce fuelwood and/or market products, while conserving and enriching soils. The
component will complement land-based production with a scaling-up of alternative value-chain
products for smallholders that are nature-positive, including, but not limited to, tourism-based
income, beekeeping, and improved cooking stoves. Central to these activities will be the
facilitation of access to market chains and financial mechanisms for establishing and
maintaining businesses. Given that these activities are designed at the core to be profitable and
promote financial sustainability, it is intended that they be replicable and sustained once GCF
funding expires.
Project management (total cost: USD 3.1 million; GCF cost: USD 2.7 million)
13. The Project Management Unit (PMU) of the CND project will be established under MOE
Rwanda/Single Project Implementation Unit (SPIU) to manage day-to-day operations of
complex programme interventions. Headed by the Project Coordinator, who will also serve as
the secretary and rapporteur of the Project Steering Committee, the PMU will be responsible for
tasks such as managing and monitoring identified risks and reporting new risks to the
accredited entity (AE) and the Project Steering Committee. The PMU will adhere to MOE
Rwanda/Government of Rwanda recruitment practices and provide quarterly progress reports.
The Project Coordinator will report to the MOE Rwanda/SPIU Coordinator as the immediate
supervisor and to the Permanent Secretary as the secondary supervisor.

=== PAGE 585 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 147
14. The PMU’s structure will comprise various specialists, including for monitoring and
evaluation, procurement, gender, financial management, communication and outreach, along
with an office manager and driver. Its staff will be selected and recruited following MOE
Rwanda/Government of Rwanda procedures, aiming for a lean management structure.
Operations will conclude once the final project evaluation report and other required documents
have been submitted to MOE Rwanda, signifying a comprehensive and organized approach to
the management of the entire programme.
15. The GCF portion of this project management cost is less than 5 per cent of the total
requested GCF funding and is compliant with the GCF Policy on Fees.
III. Assessment of performance against investment criteria
3.1 Impact potential Scale: N/A
16. The project has 1,254,24 direct beneficiaries, representing 30.9 per cent of the CND
population, and 9,260,745 indirect beneficiaries, representing almost 70 per cent of Rwanda’s
population. Additional adaptation benefits will include the training of 45,992 community
members in forest management and restoration for climate resilience. Altogether, the project
will contribute to the restoration of 5,000 ha of intact forest, 2,500 ha of protective forests,
3,346 ha of smallholder farmland, 1,000 ha of pastures and 1,500 ha of riparian linkages.
Overall, 275,617 ha of landscape could potentially be positively impacted by the project.
Although the project is focused on priority landscapes covering 275,617 ha, it is likely that
benefits due to increased adaptive capacity could feasibly extend across the full 700,000 ha
CND. The project will generate mitigation benefits by sequestering approximately 250,841 t CO
2
eq during the five-year project period, which is about 0.9 per cent of the 28.2 million t CO eq
2
reduction target in Rwanda’s Vision 2050. The total mitigation impact from reduced
deforestation, the introduction of forest restoration and adoption of improved cookstoves is
estimated to be 1,204,448 t CO eq by 2043.
2
17. The project contributes to the implementation of Rwanda’s updated nationally
determined contribution (NDC) (2020) commitments. It is also aligned with the country’s Green
Growth and Climate Resilience Strategy and other national policies. The proposal objectives are
also well aligned with the country’ National Forest Policy and related plans for reversing trends
of high deforestation.
18. With support from the NDC Partnership, Rwanda now has a single NDC implementation
framework that captures both national and subnational climate actions and investments plans
and includes a strategic programme for climate resilience, scaling up renewable energy
programme, green climate fund strategic framework, public investment priorities, sector
strategic plans and district development strategies. Therefore, the proposed project is well
supported by this existing NDC implementation framework that provides an enabling
environment that will ensure climate actions undertaken are integrated into national planning.
19. The proposed project further strengthens the country’s national and subnational
adaptation priorities, approaches and plans through promoting ecosystem-based adaptation
while utilizing climate science, effective landscape planning, policies, cross-sectoral
coordination and management in addressing climate risks and adaptation benefits.
20. The project in general seeks outcomes at a range of levels (from national through to
catchment level) across the public sector, while scaling up lessons and initiatives from aligned
programming. It will build the capacity of MOE Rwanda (AE) and other related agencies and
stakeholders to coordinate and collaborate more effectively to help accelerate subnational and
local climate action. It is envisaged that these funds will also crowd in additional private sector

=== PAGE 586 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 148
capital (e.g. cookstoves and forest plantations) while enabling the government to implement the
adaptation interventions. However, without a clear private sector framework or plan, this might
be challenging to implement. Nonetheless, Rwanda has a GCF country programme and strategic
framework and has managed GCF funded projects and programmes.
21. Furthermore, the project clearly articulates the alignment, additionality and/or
complementarity with several ongoing or planned programmes funded by significant
international and multilateral agencies (e.g. World Bank, Global Environment Facility and
United Nations Development Programme, etc.), which reflects on the experience and track
record of MOE Rwanda to deliver on this project interventions.
3.2 Paradigm shift potential Scale: N/A
22. By utilizing integrated landscape and ecosystem-based adaptation approaches in
addressing climate change impacts in Rwanda, the project offers myriad opportunities for
upscaling and replication to similar ecological zones across the country. This approach to land-
use planning and management is entirely new for Rwanda and will restore and sustain varied
ecosystem services for both adjacent and nationwide populations. The project coordination and
collaboration efforts across both geographic and sectoral boundaries, while mainstreaming
climate risks in management planning, represents a fundamental paradigm shift for land-use
planning and management in Rwanda.
23. The project has the potential to contribute to the regulatory frameworks and policies for
driving climate investments in the forest and renewable energy sectors. The project will finance
the development of the integrated land-use plan, which will be adopted by all ten CND districts
as a framework for seeking synergies between rural livelihoods and forest and biodiversity
protections, reconciling land-use conflicts that arise, and guiding development decisions and
climate change adaptation. It will also update the National Land Use Master Plan to ensure it
incorporates climate resiliency and is accurate and relevant to local contexts. The adoption of an
integrated land-use planning approach helps to better reconcile cross-sectoral trade-off’s and
improve climate adaptation planning in the CND; this approach will prove a successful model
for application in other regions of Rwanda and other forest/farming landscapes beyond. In
addition, revising two national park management plans to include climate concerns will serve as
a model for the remaining parks of Rwanda, as well as for the East Africa region.
24. Overall, the project’s efforts in shifting policy, practice and collaborative learning
processes symbolize a fundamental change towards climate-resilient development pathways in
Rwanda, with implications for broader regional application.
3.3 Sustainable development potential Scale: N/A
25. The project is closely aligned with several Sustainable Development Goals. Key
environmental benefits include restoration of degraded lands to reduce erosion, sedimentation,
and landslide risks; the planting of native trees to enhance biological connectivity; and
mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions through both increased carbon sequestration and fuel-
efficient cookstove technologies.
26. Social benefits extend to more than a million people, focusing on increased awareness of
climate change, empowerment of the rural poor (with an emphasis on women’s participation),
and creation of social capital through collaborative adaptation strategies. The project aims to
significantly reduce poverty and inequality. It will provide economic co-benefits such as
increased agricultural productivity, employment opportunities for around 24,212 households,
modern beekeeping practices yielding significant income, and a net present value (NPV) of USD
369 million over 20 years from forest restoration and other activities. Private capital

=== PAGE 587 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 149
investment is also targeted, thus fostering a “triple bottom line” that balances social,
environmental and economic benefits. Emphasis on gender-sensitive impacts ensures that
women are actively engaged in planning and decision-making, leading to increased income,
improved health and nutrition, and strengthened leadership and entrepreneurship skills.
27. Overall, the project offers a comprehensive and strategic approach to sustainable
development, thereby promoting climate resilience, economic growth, social cohesion and
gender equality within the CND region.
3.4 Needs of the recipient Scale: N/A
28. The project proposal interventions were designed from key findings and
recommendations of a climate change vulnerability assessment of the selected project
geographical area (see annex 2). Climate exposure, sensitivity, adaptive capacity, impacts and
barriers as well the greenhouse gas emissions profile were established and either quantified or
supported with reference to scientific publications. Further, climate change impacts on the
target sectors as well as size and economic and social development of the target population,
including critical barriers to reduce their vulnerability, are elaborated herein. The proposed
interventions are targeted to match the identified barriers. The vulnerability of the target
sectors is quantified to the extent possible, however, gender disaggregation is covered in
qualitative terms only.
29. The CND landscape districts support nearly one third of Rwanda’s population on barely
one fifth of its land base. The total population is 1,598,536, of which women account for 52.2 per
cent. Through the project interventions, targeted vulnerable groups will attain more climate-
resilient livelihoods from reduced exposure to landslides, floods and soil erosion and more
knowledge on climate risks, the value of forests and forest ecosystems, climate adaptation
options, access to quality indigenous and agroforestry materials, and improved ecosystem
services.
3.5 Country ownership Scale: N/A
30. MOE Rwanda, which is the AE for this proposal, clearly played a pivotal role in defining
and drafting the proposal stakeholder engagement report and plan (see annex 7) as it is aligned
with Rwanda’s GCF country programme stakeholder engagement strategic framework. In its
country programme, Rwanda articulated how it will conduct stakeholder engagement at the
readiness stage and in delivering GCF concepts, projects and programmes. This process has
provided Rwanda with an overarching framework that supports its stakeholder engagement
processes, which is clearly seen in this proposal. This framework can support the strengthening
of local climate action from national to local levels with clear feedback loops and avenues for
incorporating learning.
31. The proposal indicates that a detailed stakeholder and gender analysis were conducted,
augmented by extensive consultations of various actors from national, subnational and local
levels. A range of stakeholders from the public and civil society were consulted, in addition to
government agencies at all levels that will be engaged throughout the project cycle, cutting
across all key sectors and scale. The general concern relates to local ownership and the transfer
of knowledge that can sustain interventions after the project closure. It would be ideal if
Indigenous knowledge and technology transfer is well factored into implementation.

3.6 Efficiency and effectiveness Scale: N/A
32. Utilizing grant financing reflects the public good character of the investments, the
project aims to create a model that overcomes barriers to private sector investment in
Rwanda’s forestry sector. With an economic internal rate of return of 43.32 per cent and a
financial internal rate of return of 42 per cent, the project is estimated to generate an NPV of
more than USD 120.48 million over 20 years, which translates to USD 64 per direct beneficiary.
The mitigation cost is estimated to be USD 43.84 per t CO eq. Implementing best practices for
2

similar initiatives and sets the stage for potential replication in other regions. Its community-
focused approach, including measures to develop economically viable units, contributes to a
threefold increase in net economic benefits compared to a scenario without the project.
IV. Assessment of consistency with GCF safeguards and policies
4.1 Environmental and social safeguards
33. Project background: The project aims to increase resilience of vulnerable rural
communities in the Rwandan side of the CND by building capacity for integrated planning and
management through forest and landscape restoration and reducing demand for fuelwood. The
project will involve the formulation and implementation of plans (i.e. integrated district land-
use plans and enhancements of general management plans of national parks), coordination with
various agencies, capacity-building, and physical interventions on the ground. This includes
afforestation/reforestation of protected forest and private landholdings, installation of soil
conservation measures, ecological interventions such as fern removal in natural forests and
restoration of degraded forests in Gishwati-Mukura National Park, production and distribution
of fuel-efficient cookstoves, beekeeping activities, and support for the value chains of these
enterprises. Among the environmental and social (E&S) co-benefits are the enhancement of the
unique, endemic biodiversity of the area through decreased sedimentation, improved water
quality and recharge, reduced erosion, decrease in loss of soil organic matter as a result of forest
restoration and establishment of connectivity between the forests across the CND landscape.
The project is also expected to contribute to the empowerment of the women and youth in the
target areas.
34. E&S risk category and safeguards instrument: The overall project E&S risk category is
Category B (moderate). The Secretariat confirms the proposed E&S risk category since the
project is, in itself, an environmental and social enhancement project. The potential adverse E&S
risks and impacts will mainly come from the implementation of ground activities, are expected
to be mostly minimal and highly localized and can be avoided/mitigated through careful design
and the application of generally accepted mitigation measures and standards. The Secretariat
conforms to the assigned risk category and it is within the accreditation level of the AE. A partial
environmental and social impact assessment and environmental and social management
framework (ESMF) have been prepared for the project.
35. Compliance with the GCF ESS standards: The paragraphs below provide a brief
description of the programme’s compliance with ESS standards.
36. ESS 1 (Assessment and management of environmental and social risks and
impacts): The ESMF discussed the baseline socioeconomic conditions of the project area. It has
also provided a general assessment of the risks and impacts of the project. The assessment
included an indication of the positive and negative components of the activities and
subactivities, the consequence of the impact, the probability that the impact will occur, the
duration for which the impacts are expected to occur, and the overall significance of the impact.

=== PAGE 589 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 151
Nevertheless, given that much of the project activities cannot yet be fully specified in terms of
location, ownership, design and approach and will only be identified and fully specified through
consultations and coordination with various stakeholders during project implementation, the
ESMF provided the basis for identifying the risks and impacts of the subprojects and defining
the processes and procedures to be applied in assessing and managing the risks and impacts of
individual project activities during implementation. The major anticipated negative impacts of
the proposed activities and subactivities include, but are not limited to: disproportionate
distribution of project benefits, potential for gender-based violence (GBV), risks related to
labour and working conditions, community health and safety, potential for introduction of
invasive species and pests on planted seedlings, water use at nurseries diverting from other
uses, use of pesticides and fertilizers in seedling production, destabilization and erosion during
construction/reconstruction of terraces, land classification that impact access and introduce
restrictions, increased exposure to disease/vector-borne illnesses, potential for negative
human-wildlife interactions, and environmental risks related to the supply chain. Among the
mitigating measures include a commitment to stakeholder engagement, a process of consent,
training on sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (SEAH), establishing a grievance redress
mechanism (GRM), adhering to the labour and safety laws and international good practices,
providing training on invasive species management, providing oversight in the supply chain,
and adoption of practices to reduce the use of chemicals and production of wastes.
37. ESS 2 (Labour and working conditions): The project will likely require the hiring of
professionals, service personnel and assistants, and activities on the ground such as terracing,
removal of ferns and reforestation/afforestation activities will require the hiring of field
workers and labourers. Risks associated with these activities include, but are not limited to, the
potential for SEAH in the hiring process or at work, forced labour, child labour, and exposure to
occupational health and safety hazards. Workers may be exposed to hazardous working
environments such as steep slopes, disease vectors in standing waters, safety hazards in the
fabrication/production of stoves, and exposure to bee stings in honey production, among other
things. The project will ensure proper labour and working conditions are provided to workers
(e.g. in forest camps), and trainings on labour and occupational health and safety standards will
be undertaken. A Code of Conduct as regards worker safety and security will also be reflected in
contract documents. Moreover, the project will not support activities that include the use of
forced labour, human trafficking and child labour. During implementation, risks and potential
impacts related to labour and working conditions will be further assessed and managed through
the development of a labour and working conditions risk management plan, including ensuring
that workers have access to a GRM.
38. ESS 3 (Resource efficiency and pollution control): The nature of the proposed
interventions does not entail the use of substantial amounts of fuel, water, electricity or raw
materials, except for the operation of nurseries (for its water requirement) and the production
and distribution of cookstoves (for raw materials and electricity). The project will however
promote the increased use of energy-efficient cooking stoves to lessen the impact on forest
resources for fuel. During implementation, further review on resource efficiency and pollution
control risks will be undertaken to assess and manage issues as regards water use and water
availability, use of pesticides and fertilizers, potential for soil loss, soil erosion and slope
destabilization, and use of raw materials and waste generation in the cook stove
fabrication/production and distribution. The project will also ensure raw materials are from
sustainable sources and will establish measures to minimize production waste and maximize
distribution efficiency of stoves. Appropriate management measures will be developed upon
screening and assessment of these risks.
39. ESS 4 (Community health, safety and security): The project activities could have
community health, safety and security issues, which include potential for increased exposure to
vector-borne diseases should ecological balance be altered or stagnant water develop as a result
of the reforestation/afforestation and fern removal activities in the area (which may increase

=== PAGE 590 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 152
the population of certain disease vectors and insect pests). Some of the mitigating measures
include proper drainage design of terraces. There could also be possibility for human–wildlife
conflict in areas where fruit trees are planted, which may inadvertently increase physical
interactions with wildlife that could result in crop loss or physical injury both to humans and
wildlife. The risk related to the presence of migrant labour is considered low given that the
project will hire residents from surrounding communities. Nevertheless, the activities will be
assessed more closely with regard to such risks, with measures to be discussed and determined
in consultation with the communities during implementation.
40. ESS 5 (Land acquisition and involuntary resettlement): The project does not include
any activities that will require resettlement or involuntary taking of land. However, project
activities could facilitate a potential loss of access to lands given that the
afforestation/reforestation activities could result in stricter enforcement of land use and park
laws in changes to rules of access or land classification. To address this, the project will not
establish protective forests on lands used for food production. On-farm afforestation will not
involve the acquisition of lands, land rights or land-use rights through expropriation or other
compulsory procedures and will comply with the country’s legal system. Communities will be
engaged in an inclusive and participatory manner and will be part of the planning and
afforestation processes, and agreements on land rights and responsibilities will be developed
with them. An access restrictions mitigation process framework is developed and will be
implemented as required.
41. ESS 6 (Biodiversity conservation and sustainable management of living natural
resources): The project intends to enhance the region’s ecosystem to reduce the vulnerability
of communities to climate change impacts. For instance, the proposed interventions on
protected forests will be restoration (e.g. restoration of the 500 ha of degraded forest in GMNP,
and the fern removal covering 4,500 ha of Nyungwe National Park, while the proposed
interventions in the Stepping Stones and Landscapes Linkages (located outside of the parks)
will be composed of the protection of isolated forest patches and afforestation on steep slopes
and riparian areas supplemented with agroforestry activities to enhance ecosystem services.
Nevertheless, care should be exercised in implementing these activities to ensure that negative
impacts such as potential for the introduction of alien or invasive species, pests and pathogens
from poorly managed nurseries are adequately addressed. During project implementation,
consultations with communities and stakeholders will aid in determining the selection of
appropriate species suitable to the locality.
42. GCF Indigenous Peoples Policy and ESS 7 (Indigenous Peoples): The AE recognizes
that while there are historically marginalized groups as well as "Categories C, D and E, groups"
that may meet the GCF criteria for Indigenous Peoples that could potentially be included in the
project area, the screening so far has indicated that Indigenous Peoples have not been found in
the project area. Given that specific sites will be selected for project activities during project
implementation, each subproject will be subject to more in-depth screening for impacts to
historically marginalized peoples, with particular attention to the GCF criteria of Indigenous
Peoples, during project implementation. The AE will conduct a screening for subprojects as
outlined in the “Screening for Presence of and Risks to Historically Marginalized Groups” to
evaluate the characteristics of historically marginalized and Categories C, D and E people.
Should the screening process identify Indigenous Peoples, then the subactivity will require a
historically marginalized peoples plan. The AE also recognizes that there are potential barriers
to integrating historically marginalized peoples into the project. Nevertheless, there is interest
in working with historically marginalized groups to identify how traditional livelihoods like
beekeeping can be adapted and promoted and how negative impacts on these livelihoods will be
mitigated. The AE has included in the project the hiring of an ESS specialist and community
engagement specialist to minimize risks as well including a commitment to stakeholder
engagement, free, prior and informed consent and the setting up of a project-level GRM. In line
with its roles and functions, the GCF Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group (IPAG) is available to

=== PAGE 591 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 153
provide advice to the AE, which is also encouraged to share emerging good practices and
success stories with IPAG.
43. ESS 8 (Cultural Heritage): The physical interventions (i.e. afforestation, reforestation
and terracing, etc.) will be undertaken in mountainous areas where there are few human
settlements. The preliminary screening of target areas also indicated that it is not expected that
the project activities will disturb any cultural heritage sites. Nevertheless, the project has
developed a chance find procedure to cover chance encounters of artefacts during project
implementation.
44. Institutional implementation arrangements: As the AE, MOE Rwanda will oversee
and monitor the management and implementation of the project. The Wildlife Conservation
Society (WCS) and RFA will serve as EEs for the project through a project cooperation
agreement. All work will be coordinated by the PMU and supported by other relevant
government agencies, including the National Land Authority and the RWB within MOE Rwanda.
The PMU will have oversight of the day-to-day operations of the project, including monitoring
and evaluation. It will engage specialists (e.g. Environmental and Social Safeguards Specialist,
Invasive Species Specialist, Community Engagement Specialist, Behaviour Change Specialist,
Gender Specialist, etc.) that will screen for the potential environmental and social risks and
impacts and develop management measures for proposed activities. The PMU will also be
responsible for coordination on trainings for all project EEs. As regards safety, a Labour and
Safety Coordinator will also oversee working conditions in the field. The project will also engage
Community Engagement Specialists and Labour and Safety Officers.
45. Stakeholder engagement and GRM: The project benefited substantively from an
extensive stakeholder consultation process, which started during the project conceptualization.
A Stakeholder Engagement Plan has also been prepared to engage the stakeholders throughout
project implementation. The project will have a project-level GRM, which is described in the
ESMF. The GRM is independent of governmental judicial procedures. The project also allows
access to the GCF independent redress mechanism. In line with the GCF Indigenous Peoples
Policy, the GCF Indigenous Peoples’ focal point will be available for assistance at any stage,
including before a claim has been made.
46. Sexual exploitation, sexual abuse, and sexual harassment safeguarding: The SEAH
safeguarding approach proposed by the AE is considered by the Secretariat to be in compliance
with the SEAH provisions pursuant to the revised GCF Environmental and Social Policy. The
project identifies that all project components may exacerbate the existing power differentials
and expose the project beneficiaries to potential SEAH risk. The AE will take a number of
mitigation measures to prevent and manage SEAH, including ensuring that all staff are trained
on survivor-centred approaches to address SEAH, and that the Human Resources and
Administration Officer and the ESS Specialist of the project will work together to develop a
Security and Risk Management Plan to prevent SEAH incidences. The project’s Gender Specialist
and Community Engagement Specialist will develop training on SEAH prevention, GBV
programming and survivor-centred approach. The project will also safeguard against SEAH
through a Code of Conduct that explicitly indicates zero tolerance for GBV. This Code of Conduct
will be shared with all personnel and used for training all employees. In addition to the
prevalence of GBV in the target country, the project also recognizes that the influx of funds and
activities, combined with power dynamics, may disproportionately affect women, youth,
historically marginalized people, and others in the poverty categories of Rwanda. As the specific
locations and beneficiaries will be determined during full implementation, each subproject will
be screened to avoid any subproject that may aggravate risks of GBV and SEAH. The project will
respond to SEAH incidents through GRMs at the AE, EE, and project levels. Training will be
organized for all project staff, implementing partners, key service providers and other partner
organizations to identify and regularly assess SEAH risks along the project cycle as well as

=== PAGE 592 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 154
ensure that both the AE and all the EEs respond to SEAH incidents with survivor-centred and
gender responsive approaches.
4.2 Gender policy
47. The AE has provided a gender assessment and action plan therefore complies with the
requirements of the GCF Gender Policy.
48. The gender assessment provided demonstrates the commitment of Rwanda to
advancing gender equality and women’s empowerment. The assessment shows that Rwanda
has a strong political commitment to promoting gender equality, reflected in its policy and legal
framework and various sectoral strategies. It is the first country to have a majority female
Parliament, with 61 per cent of these positions being held by women, and has established
through its constitution a minimum of 30 per cent female representation in public governance.
The country has also made international commitments such as ratifying and implementing the
Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination against Women, the Beijing
Platform for Action and the Maputo Protocol on the Rights of Women in Africa. An institutional
framework for coordinating and ensuring oversight of gender equality and women’s
empowerment is in place, which mainly rests with the Ministry of Gender and Family
Promotion. The Ministry is mandated to coordinate the implementation of the national gender
policy and advocacy on gender issues, a gender monitoring office and the National Women’s
Council. All ministries and public institutions have gender focal points. However, there is
divergence between the frameworks in place and implementation on the ground due to
challenges such as lack of financial resources and technical capacity within the various
ministries as well as existing norms and practices that run contrary to equality principles and
practices.
49. The gender assessment was conducted through desk review and stakeholder
consultation. Additional stakeholder consultation will be conducted at national, district and
project site level in order to further adapt project activities to the local context. The assessment
indicates that women and men have different roles and responsibilities within society and
households. These roles rigidly set women as caregivers and homemakers, while men are
considered breadwinners engaging in income-generating activities, wage employment and
decision-making. Women own less land, have less access to extension services and financial
support (loans), and are less educated and able to gain experience in handling money. Women
rely more on informal sources of loans as they do not usually have collateral to put up to access
loans from financial institutions. Women engage and represent 66 per cent of the agricultural
workforce; however, they occupy 19.7 of the paid jobs. Women’s roles in afforestation and
agroforestry is also curtailed by their lack of ownership and or land rights. Lack of land rights
hinders the financial benefits women can get from resources on land such as trees. Women
mostly use trees that provide little commercial value; rather they are focused on fulfilling their
household needs through fuelwood, fodder, bean poles and fruits. Discussion with women had
indicated that women observed shortages of fuelwood, fodder and wood suitable to their bean
poles, and also that there is declining soil fertility and crop yields. Fuelwood also is the main
source for cooking, which has health hazards for women, and gaining access to cleaner,
improved cook stoves is a challenge. Men usually decide not to spend money to purchase the
improved cook stoves that can directly address the multiple challenges faced by women.
Female-headed households are identified as much more vulnerable to climate change impacts
compared to male-headed households owing to the prevalent gender inequality. Engagement in
alternative source of incomes for women poses its own challenges to women, one of which is
affordability of required inputs, and this is particularly so for the beekeeping sector. The
interest of the government is this area is also high, and investments have taken place, but only
23 per cent of women engaged in the sector.

=== PAGE 593 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 155
50. The action plan includes activities that will address the challenges identified through the
gender assessment. Activities contain corresponding indicators, targets, gender expertise and
budget while also including timelines for each of the actions. The project will direct investments
to the areas of equal access to resources (e.g. land), services (finance), capacity development,
decision-making and also the participation of women in management, as beneficiaries/partners
and as critical stakeholders in processes. Project interventions will respond to and address the
growing pressure on natural resources, thus ensuring that the resilience and adaptive capacities
of communities, including that of women and disadvantaged people, are built. The gender action
plan is focused on ensuring (1) climate adaptation programmes and land-use planning address
the priorities of women and youth; (2) women, youth and marginalized households have
increased capacity to effectively engage in and benefit from forest management and forest
restoration; (3) women, youth and marginalized households have improved capacity to engage
in green jobs and livelihood activities; and (4) monitoring and evaluation effectively measures
how women, youth and marginalized people are benefiting to enable the adaptive management
of the project. A capacity-building component that focuses on strengthening cooperatives and
village savings and loans institutions through gender mainstreaming across decision-making,
membership, and products and services is included to ensure women are able to benefit from
and engage in all aspects of the project. Private landowners who will be willing to engage in land
afforestation activities will create private forest management units, which will then be assisted
in forming and registering cooperatives that are at least 50 per cent women. Further, the
selection of tree species will take into consideration women’s usage and priorities. Women will
be engaged and supported through knowledge acquisition, trainings, and skills development
processes so that they benefit from the project implementation, particularly focusing on critical
challenges such as rights to land and access to decision-making positions. Further, the challenge
of rights to land will be addressed through advocacy work with men and local judiciary systems.
This will be complemented by activities that will advocate for women’s land rights and access to
redress mechanisms. The project will engage community leaders and women and men
community influencers to further promote equal and fair control of resources to mitigate the
risk of men taking control over incomes earned by women.
51. There are three recommendations to the AE. The first recommendation is that the AE
needs to ensure that gender issues are mainstreamed across all components of the project; this
is lacking for component 3 (output 3.1 of the gender action plan), which presents many
important opportunities to address gender issues. Secondly, the AE needs to refine and clearly
show what outcomes it intends to achieve as a result of the interventions. Activity 3.1.1 in the
funding proposal states the following regarding the composition of administrative committees:
"Note that gender consideration is mandatory (at least 30% women)". It is not clear if 30 per
cent refers to “women in decision-making bodies” or “membership of women in cooperatives”,
or both. These results are different in nature and should be captured independently. The AE
should provide clarification in this regard. Thirdly, as part of its expressed commitment to do so,
the AE should consistently collect data and report in a sex-disaggregated manner on the gender
action plan.

4.3.3. Programme-specific execution risks (Medium risk)
54. Co-financing: We acknowledge the sizable amount of co-financing totalling USD

4.3.4. Compliance risk (medium risk)
57. MOE Rwanda, in its capacity as AE, confirmed that it has conducted a risk assessment of
money laundering and terrorist financing (ML/TF) in relation to project implementation. The
probability of occurrence was assessed as ‘low’, and the impact severity in the event of
occurrence was assessed as ‘medium’.
58. MOE Rwanda confirmed that co-financiers have been identified based on their existing
mandates and activities implemented in the CND region. Co-financiers’ commitments will serve
as a basis of MOE Rwanda engagement during the project implementation. During
implementation, annual work plans for the project will be adjusted in collaboration with the EE,
and all co-financiers are to align with all activities. MOE Rwanda, per its oversight role, will
ensure that all of these stakeholders commit during planning to their co-financing and report
this in the annual performance reports submitted to GCF.
59. MOE Rwanda indicated that the Government of Rwanda currently has robust measures
to fight ML/TF risks (e.g. law N° 001/FIC/2022 on regulations relating to anti-money
laundering and countering the financing terrorism). The Government of Rwanda has also put in
place a special agency for this purpose, the Financial Intelligence Center (FIC), which has a clear
mission to promote financial system integrity by conducting effective financial intelligence to
counter ML/TF and related financial crimes in governmental institutions, projects and
parastatal agencies under the supervision of the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning.
Both MOE Rwanda and this project under its supervision will also comply with FIC regulations.
60. MOE Rwanda confirmed that it has an internal audit function as well as regular audits
conducted by the Office of the Auditor General to ensure the efficiency and effectiveness of
internal controls, which includes handling ML/TF risks. In addition, MOE Rwanda uses
segregation of duties within financial management processes.

=== PAGE 595 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 157
61. MOE Rwanda confirmed that it has conducted a risk assessment of prohibited practices
in relation to project implementation. The probability of occurrence was assessed as Low, and
the impact severity in the event of occurrence was assessed as Medium.
62. MOE Rwanda indicated that to ensure materials or technology procured under the
project are used only for the purposes intended and not diverted or misused for unauthorized,
improper or illicit purposes, a comprehensive set of controls will be used. This includes explicit
terms and conditions in all procurement contracts or agreements that clearly (i) state the
intended purpose of the materials or technology being provided and explicitly prohibit any
unauthorized use or diversion; and (ii) define the individuals that are authorized to access and
use the procured materials or technology. Furthermore, this will involve the implementation of
strong authentication and access controls to ensure that only approved users have access. This
refers to the record of any materials or technology procured under projects within an assets
register. The records include assets identification, the person using the material and the
location.
63. Monitoring and auditing the usage of the procured materials or technology will be
undertaken to detect any anomalies or potential misuse, including periodic site visits. Training
sessions will also be conducted to educate all stakeholders involved in the project about the
importance of adhering to the intended use of the materials or technology and the consequences
of misuse. For technologies that involve data transmission or storage, MOE Rwanda will ensure
that appropriate encryption and data protection measures are in place to safeguard sensitive
information.
64. MOE Rwanda confirmed that no projects will be undertaken in any jurisdiction or
territory that is subject to or affected by sanctions or restrictive measures per the United
Nations Security Council (UNSC) resolutions. Additionally, no individual or entity that is listed
on any UNSC sanctions list, including the United Nations Consolidated Sanctions list, will be
involved in any manner with the project or its activities, either as a counterparty, implementer
or beneficiary.
65. MOE Rwanda acknowledged that there are United Nations sanctions in the neighbouring
country of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, close to the CND. According to MOE Rwanda,
the United Nations Consolidated Sanctions List indicates approximately 20 individuals with ties
to Rwanda, a small percentage of whom may live in Rwanda. MOE Rwanda confirmed that the
United Nations Consolidated Sanctions List has been circulated internally and will be cross
checked when hiring for the project and once project sites are selected to ensure these
individuals will not be involved in any manner with the project or its activities, either as a
counterparty, implementer or beneficiary.
66. MOE Rwanda indicated that the project involves many actors for successful
implementation, including ministries, government agencies, non-governmental organizations,
subgrantees, vendors, service providers, community members and beneficiaries. MOE Rwanda
confirmed that there is specifically an intention to distribute or disburse to beneficiaries, both
directly and indirectly, commodities and other items of value such as (i) the distribution of
seedlings for trees that will produce fruits or contribute to enhancing biodiversity of farming
systems; (ii) access to improved cook stoves; as well as (iii) the option for the distribution of
bees to start honey operations. MOE Rwanda acknowledged that, as with any project infusing
large sums of money directly or indirectly with multiple actors, corruption could occur.
67. MOE Rwanda indicated that the distributions will be coordinated through procured
contractors. The contractors are hired based on the Government of Rwanda/MOE Rwanda
procurement policies, which are aligned with GCF policies and include due diligence in the
hiring and contracting process. As for direct community contracting, the intended beneficiaries
are screened and certified by local authorities in the area of project interventions, which
mitigates the risk of prohibited practices.

Proposal name: Building Resilience of Vulnerable Communities to Climate
Variability in Rwanda’s Congo Nile Divide through Forest and

I. Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
1. This funding proposal for a small-sized project in environmental and social safeguards
(ESS) category B is submitted by the Government of Rwanda as a cross-cutting project
contributing to both adaptation (92 per cent) and mitigation (8 per cent) results areas. The
Ministry of Environment of Rwanda (MOE Rwanda) (a GCF direct access entity) is the
accredited entity (AE) for the proposed project, and the executing entity (EE) is the Rwanda
Forestry Agency, with several implementing partners, including other government agencies and
the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) in Rwanda. The total cost of the funding proposal is
USD 50 million, of which USD 39 million is GCF finance and USD 11 million is co-finance from
the Government of Rwanda.
2. The project’s goal is to apply a landscape approach to reduce the exposure of
populations in Rwanda’s Congo Nile Divide (CND) landscape to the impacts of unfavourable
climatic trends and hazards intensified by climate change, including floods, landslides, soil
erosion and wildfires. This is to be achieved through integrated land-use planning and
management that allows for protecting, restoring and managing a matrix of interconnected
ecosystems, including pristine forest in protected area nodes, important landscape linkages,
pockets of forest in stepping stones, and agro-ecosystems in farmlands. Interventions in various
spatially defined target areas include forest protection and fire management, assisted natural
regeneration, afforestation of steep slopes, and support to silvopastoralism and agroforestry
and its value chains.
3. The project has three planned outcomes (see the table below), with outputs under each
outcome as well as the parties responsible for executing them (see table 5 in the funding
proposal).

5. The emphasis on utilizing the GCF investment to enhance the resilience of ecosystems
and ecosystem services is reflected in the project’s focus on new mechanisms of land-use
planning and management that consider the CND as a landscape consisting of an
interdependent mosaic of forests and farms, the management of each determining the health of
the whole. The independent Technical Advisory Panel (iTAP) believes that such an approach
(i.e. targeting project interventions on the ground based on a systematic spatial planning
process that emphasizes “ecological infrastructure” functioning as well as biodiversity)
represents best practice for enhancing ecosystem resilience. Such an approach ensures that
interventions are at sufficient scale to achieve a transformative effect: preserving landscape-
wide ecosystem processes and functions that help buffer impacts of climate change. Maximizing
connectivity is also important for maintaining the long-term health and stability of forests as
carbon sinks.
6. Adaptation impact potential: The funding proposal outlines the major climate change-
related hazards characterizing the landscape, in particular more frequent intense rainfall events
increasing floods and landslides, and worsening soil erosion that is already widespread as a
result of direct anthropogenic pressures. The project’s main adaptation benefits will accrue to

7. Indicators for the main adaptation results are as follows:
(a) 135,104 hectares (ha) of land to be brought under climate-resilient management
through targeted interventions for protection, afforestation and agroforestry (AR4):
(i) Including 121,758 ha of core protected areas, linkages and stepping stones that
will be brought under climate-risk informed planning and fire management to
maintain landscape-scale ecosystem services; and
(ii) Including 13,346 ha for focused interventions (i.e. degraded forest in parks to be
restored (5,000 ha), riparian lands restored (1,500 ha), pastures brought under
silvopastoralism (1,000 ha), steep slopes afforested (2,500 ha), and farmland
with new agroforestry practices (3,346 ha));
(b) 1,254,242 people, resident in the landscape where targeted interventions will be carried
out, will benefit directly from reduced exposure to climate-intensified disasters and/or
enhanced adaptive capacity (AR 1 and 2); and
(c) 9,260,745 people, approximately two thirds of the country’s population, will benefit
indirectly from a wide-scale education and outreach programme, including radio
programming, on climate change and gender issues, climate risks, value of forests and
forest ecosystems, and climate change adaptation options.
8. Mitigation impact: The project seeks to deliver greenhouse gas (GHG) emission
reductions and removal benefits equivalent to 224,871 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (t
CO eq) during the five-year project implementation period, reaching a total of 1,084,291 t CO2
2
eq after 20 years. The estimation of reductions and removals is made based on the difference
between the projected emissions with and without the project interventions – through
improved cookstoves, and through on-the-ground interventions across a total of 13,346 ha of
land. The land-based interventions will have cross-cutting benefits, since they contribute to core
indictor 4 on hectares of land to be brought under climate-resilient management, as well as
bringing mitigation benefits.
9. The following activities will contribute to achieving this mitigation potential: (i) assisted
natural regeneration (ANR) in 4,500 ha of Nyungwe National Park through invasive fern
removal; (ii) restoration of 500 ha of degraded forest through ANR in Gishwati-Mukura National
Park; (iii) afforestation on 2,500 ha of public and private land with a slope >55 per cent; (iv)
planting 1,500 ha of protective forest in riparian zones (public and private); (v) implementing
erosion control and agroforestry practices on 3,346 ha of smallholder farmland; (vi)
implementing silvopastoralism on 1,000 ha in the Gishwati area; and (vii) adoption of improved
cookstoves by 8,500 households. Indicators for achievement of these targets are included in the
project logical framework in section E.3 of the funding proposal.
10. The methodology for calculating GHG emission reductions and carbon sinks mirrors two
approved consolidated methodologies for the A/R CDM, AR-ACM0003 and AR-AMS0007. This is
considered a good practice because the applicability conditions of the methodologies are
appropriate to the project conditions. The methodology is clear and conservative, considers the
relevant guidance from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, and was used in an
appropriate, clear and transparent manner when estimating the mitigation potential for each
activity.

11. With regard to monitoring and reporting mitigation benefits, annex 22 proposes a clear

Furthermore, the activities as presented in annex 22 are not reflected in annex 11 (monitoring
and evaluation plan_rev August 2023). According to its updated nationally determined
contribution (NDC) (2020, page 6)1 Rwanda has already developed a national measurement,

support or contribute to enhancing the functioning of this system across the country.

1.2 Paradigm shift potential Scale: N/A
13. The proposed project is designed to bring about a paradigm shift away from the current
situation of fragmented, unplanned decisions and a collection of isolated sector-by-sector
projects that fail to take into account evolving climate risk and allow continued degradation.
Instead, a new approach of integrated land use planning and management is promoted that
preserves ecological connectivity across the landscape and helps maximize valuable ecosystem
services for buffering the impacts of climate change. The new approach is based on
international best practice and considers the CND as a landscape consisting of an
interdependent mosaic of production and protected lands, the health of which is completely
interconnected.
14. The idea behind the project is that a new holistic, climate-smart, evidence-based
approach to planning and development will enable systematic, ecosystem-based, multi-sector
analysis of land-use tradeoffs. Focusing on this larger scale, with coordination across both
geographic and sectoral boundaries, while mainstreaming climate risks in management
planning, represents a fundamental paradigm shift for land-use planning and management in
Rwanda. Success in putting such a system into place could represent a crucial first step in
reversing the previous negative feedback loop of ecosystem degradation to achieve a more
positive, climate-resilient system.
15. Utilizing integrated landscape management and ecosystem-based adaptation
approaches in addressing climate change impacts in Rwanda offers a myriad of opportunities
for scaling up and replication to similar ecological zones across the country. The project also has
the potential to contribute to the regulatory frameworks and policies for driving climate
investments in the forest and renewable energy sectors. The project will finance the
development of an integrated land-use plan, which will be adopted by all 10 CND districts as a
framework for seeking synergies between rural livelihoods and forest and biodiversity
protection, reconciling land-use conflicts that arise, and guiding development decisions and
climate change adaptation. It will also update the National Land Use Master Plan, ensuring it
incorporates climate resilience and local plans.
16. Systematic conservation planning: Although biodiversity conservation is considered a
co-benefit of the project rather than a core focus, the project makes innovative use of systematic
conservation planning to identify spatial areas in the landscape that are targeted for restoration,
afforestation and agroforestry activities. This includes work to restore national parks as the
core of an interconnected system, with landscape linkages and stepping stones identified for
interventions to promote connectivity between remaining areas of natural habitat. Optimizing
this kind of mosaic of land uses with management actions for protection, restoration and
sustainable use helps to maximize the functionality of landscape-wide ecosystem services such

interconnected.

17. Innovative financial mechanisms: The project also includes an output to establish
long-term plans for CND financial sustainability post-GCF by employing a technical advisor to
support the establishment of innovative mechanisms such as those identified in the Biodiversity
Finance Plan and also to refine existing financing mechanisms (for example, integrating climate
resilience principles into the existing successful and growing Tourism Revenue Sharing
Program). Support will be provided to beneficiaries of the project in applying to the existing
Community Adaptation Facility within the Rwanda Green Fund (FONERWA). The Government
of Rwanda, represented by the Rwanda Development Board, is also in advanced stages of
negotiation with the World Bank for establishing a wildlife bond, potentially a gorilla
conservation bond, modelled on the successfully established rhino conservation bond in South
Africa, with interest shown by impact investors.
18. Overall, based on the above, the paradigm shift potential of the project is assessed as
medium to high.
1.3 Sustainable development potential Scale: N/A
19. The proposed project is aligned with the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable
Development, including significant contributions towards Rwanda’s efforts to meet Sustainable
Development Goal (SDG) 5 (Gender Equality), SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 15 (Life on
Land), and will contribute to the achievement of SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG
3 (Good Health and Well-being) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).
20. Environmental co-benefits: Key environmental co-benefits (beyond the core benefits
related to ecosystem-based adaptation) include restoration of soil fertility through
silvopastoralism and regenerative mixed-use agroforestry, and the enhancement of biodiversity
through planting 50 per cent native tree species. Promotion of improved cookstoves using
significantly less fuel will contribute to relieving pressure on the remaining indigenous forest.
21. The iTAP was surprised to see the relatively low target of 50 per cent (30 per cent on
private land and 70 per cent on public land) in the use of indigenous tree species in
afforestation, reforestation and agroforestry interventions. The AE explained that exotic species
are more suitable for afforestation of steep slopes, where they can easily establish themselves,
“but this does not mean that exclusively exotic species will be used on such sites; there will be a
mixture of both wherever applicable. In addition, while establishing blocks in the Participatory
Forest Management Units, indigenous species will be used to separate one block from another.
Indigenous species will be given due consideration in agroforestry to create positive
interactions in the farm as well as promoting native species, avoiding monoculture and
benefiting from their positive impacts in terms of resilience.”
22. It is understood that there is often a preference for fast-growing, easily available and
usually cheaper species like eucalyptus, pine and alnus for urgent needs such as slope
stabilization and fuelwood, and also that a balance needs to be struck between promoting
indigenous trees species and being responsive to farmers’ wishes. At the same time, the project
could potentially make more of the opportunity to rekindle traditional knowledge about
indigenous species and their uses, and to build the nursery supply chain for quality native
planting material given the vast superiority of indigenous tree species in terms of their multiple
benefits, non-invasiveness, positive impact on soil and water quality, and resistance to pests and
diseases that may worsen with a warming climate.
23. Social and health co-benefits: In enabling the transition to more climate-resilient and
productive livelihood models, the project aims to increase household incomes and the
nutritional status of families. It is expected that significant social capital will be created through

=== PAGE 604 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 166
beneficiaries’ participation in co-designing and co-managing a range of adaptation strategies,
with an emphasis on women’s participation. Social cohesiveness will also be enhanced through
the strengthening of joint saving and lending systems. Social benefits will also accrue to indirect
beneficiaries, for example those listening to radio programming that leads to increased
awareness of climate change, or of opportunities for climate-adaptive agroforestry and agri-
processing.
24. Economic co-benefits: Inequality and poverty will be addressed through increased
financial inclusion and improved economic opportunities, especially for women, youth and
historically marginalized groups. Forest and landscape restoration in the CND will bring
economic benefits, since soil erosion control measures, protective forests on public lands, and
agroforestry on private lands will all increase agricultural productivity and associated income.
The project will create direct and indirect employment opportunities, benefiting an anticipated
24,212 households and stimulating the local economy. Private capital will be leveraged to invest
in value chains, including those for improved cookstoves, irrigation pumps and beehives, as well
as honey, woodlots, macadamia, avocado and vegetable production and processing.
25. Gender benefits: The project aims to achieve positive outcomes around access to
resources, improved livelihoods, and income generation opportunities and capacities for
women. With support from a dedicated gender specialist, the project will engage women in
project planning, investment and decision-making. It is envisaged that women will respond to
incentives that address their families’ basic needs, such as better health and nutrition, linked to
agriculture and food security improvements. The project will also get support from non-
governmental organizations that engage men in programming and discussions to increase their
participation in household and parental responsibilities and enhance their awareness of the
importance of women’s fair access to and control of resources, including income. Women will
benefit from training and educational activities, leadership, entrepreneurship and decision-
making, as shown in annex 8 (Gender Analysis/Assessment and Gender and Social Inclusion
Action Plan).
26. The iTAP assesses sustainable development potential as high.
1.4 Needs of the recipient Scale: N/A
27. Western Rwanda and its CND region are highly vulnerable to climate change, and are
expected to experience a continuing upward trend in average annual temperatures, total annual
rainfall (with a longer dry season), and more intense rainfall events and storms and increasing
risk of flash floods, landslide, soil erosion and wildfires. Despite Rwanda’s solid economic
progress since 2000, poverty remains widespread and pervasive. Overall, 38.2 per cent of the
country’s population lives in poverty and 16 per cent in extreme poverty. Women are more
affected by poverty than men, with 47 per cent of female-headed households living in poverty
compared with 44.9 per cent of all households.
28. The CND landscape supports nearly one third of Rwanda’s population on barely one fifth
of its land base. Average population density is 736 people/square kilometre (km2), with some
districts now exceeding 1,000 people/km². The highest rates of rural poverty in the country are
reported from the CND, including its most vulnerable subsistence farmers. While high rainfall
has historically permitted generally sufficient food production, the region’s rugged topography
requires farming on extremely steep slopes. With more frequent extreme rainfall events in
recent years, this agricultural landscape is recognized as the region of Rwanda most vulnerable
to flash floods and landslides. Between 2013–2016, heavy rains generated landslides that killed
at least 174 people and destroyed the homes of more than 5,000. Landslides wipe out highly
productive raised-bed cultivation systems in the CND’s valleys and bottomlands, many hectares
of crops are washed away, and an estimated 1.5 million tonnes of fertile soil are lost annually to
erosion.

=== PAGE 605 ===
GCF/B.37/02/Add.08
Page 167
29. The funding proposal reports that during stakeholder consultations, communities
indicated several socioeconomic changes stemming from changing climate conditions. Notably,
the longer dry season and unpredictable rains have reduced agricultural yield significantly,
leading to more widespread malnutrition and extreme poverty, and farmers can barely meet
their own families’ needs. In particular, women, youth, and historically marginalized people are
feeling the impacts. As arable land is increasingly constrained, youth and historically
marginalized people have few opportunities and are more focused on survival and short-term
gains. This becomes a negative feedback loop, in which poverty leads to unsustainable practices
such as overharvesting from forests and cultivation on extremely steep slopes, with degraded
ecosystems then less able to provide services, worsening the cycle of poverty.
30. As a result, the Government of Rwanda has invested significantly in developing an
enabling policy and institutional framework for a more climate-resilient development pathway.
Yet, while adaptation is a top priority, as a least developed country, Rwanda lacks sufficient
public financial resources to implement its climate change and resilient green development
objectives. Currently there are no alternative funding options at the scale needed to secure
Rwanda’s priority forests to reduce the vulnerability of rural communities to climate risks.
Rwanda’s debt-to-gross domestic product ratio stands at 64 per cent, making further loans
difficult, and the Government of Rwanda seeks maximum concessionality from the GCF for the
urgent adaptation actions proposed under the project.
31. The Government of Rwanda recognizes that a piecemeal approach to decision-making
has exacerbated competition over scarce land resources and reduced the adaptive capacity of
both ecosystems and rural populations. Additionally, district government staff and community
members have limited technical understanding of the complex interactions between forest
structure and functions, climate change, and the provision of ecosystem services, and limited
technical capacity for complex forest monitoring. In the face of worsening climate change
impacts, there is an urgent need for a comprehensive approach that crosses siloes of
government and achieves integrated land use planning and management informed by the
evolving climate and socioeconomic conditions. The proposed interventions are well targeted to
address the identified barriers and the great needs of these vulnerable communities.
32. Overall, based on the above, the needs of the recipients are rated as high.
1.5 Country ownership Scale: N/A
33. Policy and strategy alignment: The project is closely aligned with Rwanda’s national
adaptation plan and three of its adaptation priorities: (i) promotion of non-agricultural income
generating activities; (ii) introduction of species resistant to environmental conditions; and (iii)
development of alternative sources of energy to firewood. It contributes to several priorities
identified in the 2020 NDC: promotion of afforestation/reforestation; improvement of forest
management; an integrated approach to planning and monitoring for sustainable land
management; and development of a harmonized and integrated spatial data management
system for sustainable land use management.
34. The project will support the implementation of Rwanda’s Green Growth and Climate
Resilient Strategy and the Rwanda National Strategy for Transformation (2017–2022) and is
aligned with the goals of the Rwanda National Forestry Policy 2018, the Forest Sector Strategic
Plan 2017–2022, the Strategic Plan for the Environment and Natural Resources Sector (2018–
2024) and the National Forest Management Plan 2017–2026, thus reflecting the government’s
intention to address climate change impacts and mitigation targets by improving forest
management. It is also aligned with the national Biomass Energy Strategy 2020, which aims to
ensure a more sustainable biomass supply and combustion technologies for homes and small
enterprises.

36. Roles of key entities: The proposed project was initiated by MOE Rwanda and
supported by the national designated authority, Rwanda Environment Management Authority,
due to the high vulnerability to climate change of the CND region of the country. MOE Rwanda is
well placed to oversee the project as AE since the ministry is responsible for (i) ensuring the
sustainable management of natural resources and for the development of policies, strategies
and regulations; and (ii) mobilizing resources for the development of the sector. MOE Rwanda
managed USD 10 million from the Adaptation Fund to implement the Reducing Vulnerability to

Restoration and Conservation and the “Building resilience of communities living in degraded
forests, savannahs and wetlands of Rwanda through an ecosystem management approach”
programme (funded by LDCF)5.

Authority and the National Land Use Authority. The project activities overseen by each are

commitments provided every year in the project intervention area. These are earmarked funds

the details are indicated in the Annex 4 of the budget and activities to be covered by co-
